quotes.text: I have been frustrated that, we have the majority of Republicans have enacted a state preemption on any kind of AI regulation, but then haven't actually produced anything at the federal level. So, yes, AI regulations would be better crafted at the federal level, but there's really nothing meaningful happening.

And there are going to be dramatic economic changes with artificial intelligence. We have to be talking about some kind of a dividend, some kind of benefit that the public gets, from all of the economic, wealth that will be generated through the AI boom.

I'm concerned that much of the research around this area of AI has been in the defense and intelligence realms, important to be sure, but not enough is being done specifically as it relates to protecting our democracy going forward, including at the State and local level, so the use of AI in political content. So my question is around the role of NSF, what might be done by NSF to take a more active role in researching and planning for how we better protect our democracy against nefarious uses of AI? And beyond basic research, how might NSF play a role in better preparing the American people for the misuse of AI in elections and political communications?

From deepfakes to ChatGPT, the proliferation of AI will have wide applications in political communications & huge implications for democracy.

We can & should use AI to its fullest potential, but in order to prevent nefarious uses, AI must be developed ethically & responsibly. https://t.co/5m1CNTdOCP

AI has been the hot topic in Washington DC this week. While this powerful tech has the capability to do incredible things, we also need to consider its potential to distort information. https://t.co/ItM9FWBLiy

AI is emerging as a powerful & potentially dangerous tool when used by malicious actors. Our laws need to be crystal clear to stop the spread of AI-generated misinformation. I joined @RepAdamSchiff to call on the @FEC to clear up rules on the use of generative AI in campaign ads.

Glad to see the FEC taking the effects of deepfakes on elections seriously and beginning a public comment process for potential new regulations on the use of generative AI. I joined my colleagues in calling for this step in a letter to support the Public Citizen petition.
When we talk about trustworthy AI, the use of such technology in machines in the physical world pose a danger that I'd like to dig into just a little bit further.

Dr. Bender, as an educator and researcher, do you have any thoughts on the topic of better educating Americans so we are prepared for the coming onslaught of humanlike content generated by AI? [...] Are we talking about education campaigns, for example? Can you enlighten me?

We have to create a regulatory framework … that can be adapted to the new uses and the future uses of AI. We are at the inception here. This feels to me like the beginning of the internet, when people were just trying to figure out ‘what is this going to mean’?

I am energized by what this can mean, yet I’m also concerned about our democracy. And 88 elections across the world in 2024. And bad actors wanting to manipulate the outcomes of those elections in democracies, that may not be up to speed in terms of their regulatory framework.

But steel, aluminum, and everything else that goes into powering data centers cost money. And we cannot win the global race on AI if American businesses can't afford the raw materials to build that infrastructure.

One of the clearest gaps that already exists is transparency. Right now, individuals often don't know when AI is making a decision about their lives, whether it is a loan, a job interview, or how their car responds on the road.

In the San Francisco Bay Area, Caltrain has piloted a system that uses lidar, cameras, and artificial intelligence to detect patterns of use and identify hazards at crossings in real time. [...] The system can then alert train engineers, dispatchers, and law enforcement to potential threats—helping prevent collisions before they occur.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to talk about the rapid rise of AI chatbots and the urgent need to put clear guardrails in place. [...] That is why I am introducing the CHATBOT Act. This legislation would prohibit companies from claiming or implying that a chatbot is a licensed professional through marketing or the bot's output.
AI chatbots are not and should not be treated as substitutes for licensed professionals, like doctors, therapists, lawyers, and financial advisers.

Many chatbot providers have added disclaimers, saying their products are not licensed professionals, but, Mr. Speaker, disclosures are not enough. [...] Clear rules are needed now to protect consumers, promote trust in responsible innovation, and ensure a level playing field for companies that are doing the right thing.

We’ve heard horrific stories about what can go wrong when people think AI chatbots are doctors, lawyers or financial advisors, and no family should have to worry that a chatbot claiming to be a therapist might lead their child into harm’s way. That’s why I introduced the CHATBOT Act, to prevent AI chatbots from claiming to be licensed professionals and deceiving consumers. https://t.co/psGLIgErkq

While AI chatbots may expand access to information, they are not a substitute for doctors, therapists, attorneys, or other licensed professionals. We’ve heard horrific stories about what can go wrong, and no family should have to worry that a chatbot claiming to be a therapist might lead their child into harm’s way. No one should be misled into emptying their savings by an AI financial advisor.

I am glad to see on the agenda the Affordable Innovation for the Grid Act, which focuses on using AI to improve the grid. FERC Commissioner Rosner noted last year that advanced computing tools can reduce the time it takes to perform grid interconnection studies from 2 years to a matter of days. So, Ms. Muse, are there specific ways that Congress can encourage adoption of these tools by utilities and grid operators, perhaps through a rulemaking, technical assistance, or a sharing of best practices?

As energy demand continues to grow, we need to make sure our power grid can keep up. New AI and computing technologies have enormous potential to help the power system operate more efficiently, reduce delays in connecting new energy resources to the grid, and improve reliability for communities across the country.
